body.heading: Books at walking pace
paragraphs: Before printing, every book was copied by hand. A single Bible might take a team of scribes years to produce, and books cost as much as houses. Knowledge existed, but it moved at the speed of handwriting and lived mostly in monasteries and universities.

The idea of printing with movable letters was older than Europe's famous version: printers in China were using carved wooden type by the 11th century, and Korean printers cast metal type in the 13th century, producing a book with it in 1377 that still survives.

body.heading: Gutenberg's workshop
paragraphs: Around 1440, in the German city of Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined several crafts into one system: metal letters cast in moulds so thousands could be made alike, oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and a press adapted from winemaking.

His workshop printed Bibles of real beauty — and the system spread like gossip. Within fifty years, presses operated in hundreds of European towns, and more books were printed in those decades than scribes had copied in the previous thousand years.

body.heading: What cheap books did
paragraphs: Falling prices put texts into the hands of merchants, students and eventually children. Ideas could be checked, argued with and carried across borders; scientists could build on identical copies of the same diagrams; and reformers, explorers and revolutionaries all learned to speak through print.
Every later flood of information — newspapers, paperbacks, the internet — follows the pattern Gutenberg's workshop set: make copies cheap, and the world reorganises itself around them.

takeaway: Movable type, perfected as a system by Gutenberg, cut the price of books so deeply that knowledge itself changed owners.
